network.overall_strategy: Construct ten distinct feedstock-to-target pathways using experimentally supported atmospheric precursor generation, two aqueous Strecker branches, hydroxylamine-associated aminonitrile chemistry, and four glyoxylate-based reaction systems. These are ten graph-distinct routes, not ten independent glycine-forming mechanisms: several converge on the same nitrile hydrolysis sequence, and the two brucite pathways differ in their nitrogen source. Methane, CO, CO2, ammonia, hydrogen, water, nitrate, hydroxylamine, glyoxylate, and reactive mineral inventories are boundary resources; upstream production of concentrated glyoxylate and hydroxylamine is not claimed to be solved. The hydroxylamine pathway is explicitly conditional because its proposed ternary formulation is less directly established than the observed binary-mixture chemistry. Surface aminonitrile formation is separated from hotter hydrolysis, and cyanide-containing solutions are not assumed to share reactors with metal-mediated reductive amination. Numerical scenario assumptions are distinguished from reported experimental anchors. Neutral organic formulas and NH3 provide reference-species accounting; actual protonation and carbonyl hydration depend on pH. Fe(OH)2 and FeOOH represent redox-active hydroxylated Fe(II) and Fe(III) component equivalents, not claims that pure mineral phases were identified. Mineral hosts and their required preparation are specified separately. Shared component nodes do not imply that spent iron from one experiment automatically becomes active ferroan brucite. Balanced equations are recorded in mechanism strings without repeating molecule IDs in reaction arrays. The schema lacks a coproduct role, so non-target terminal coproducts use intermediate. No molecular oxygen is required. Strong-acid reservoir-release routes, poorly resolved thiol chemistry, and ethanolamine oxidation with unverified hydrogen evolution are omitted rather than counted as equally established pathways.

reactions.name: Methane-rich electrical-discharge supply of Strecker precursors

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K receiving water; transient discharge plasma is much hotter than the bulk gas and liquid
conditions.other: Gas-water interface exposed to intermittent electrical discharge over days. Methane and ammonia are substantial local gas constituents; hydrogen can also be present initially. Condensation and rainfall collect soluble products in anoxic pools. Subsequent concentration and retention require replenishment, sheltered pore water, and suppression of HCN volatilization; a permanently reducing global atmosphere is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Nonselective radical and ionic gas chemistry generates aldehydes and cyanide, followed by aqueous capture. One atom-balanced precursor-production channel is 2 CH4 + NH3 + H2O -> CH2O + HCN + 5 H2. This equation records a possible net channel, not the complete discharge product distribution or a measured 1:1 formaldehyde:HCN yield.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1953, 1957) established discharge-driven amino-acid production and the central role of aqueous aldehyde/cyanide chemistry. Johnson et al. (2008) confirmed substantial glycine production in methane/ammonia-rich apparatus configurations. Electrical energy, rather than a mineral catalyst, activates the gases. Laboratory precursor production is well supported, but atmospheric persistence, capture efficiency, and accumulation to useful concentrations remain environmental boundary conditions.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-rich CO discharge supply of Strecker precursors

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K receiving water; localized nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Reducing CO/H2/NH3 gas in contact with water vapor and a collecting aqueous phase. An H2:CO molar ratio of approximately 4:1 is an illustrative reducing scenario, not a literature-derived universal threshold. Aqueous products must be collected before photolysis or dilution dominates.

reactions.mechanism: Energetic reduction and nitrogen incorporation produce carbonyl and cyanide inventories. A balanced selected channel is 2 CO + NH3 + H2 -> CH2O + HCN + H2O. The actual discharge also makes competing products and does not impose the displayed product ratio.
reactions.reasoning: Schlesinger and Miller (1983) demonstrated strong dependence of amino-acid and precursor production on the H2 content of CO-containing atmospheres. This route is chemically distinct upstream from methane discharge but converges on the same aqueous Strecker reactions. The numerical gas ratio is a scenario assumption; neither spontaneous thermal conversion at 300 K nor a high yield in hydrogen-poor CO atmospheres is asserted.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-rich CO2 discharge supply of Strecker precursors

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K receiving water; localized nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Transient H2-rich CO2/NH3 atmosphere or local gas-water system. An H2:CO2 molar ratio of approximately 4:1 is an illustrative scenario rather than a validated optimum. Rapid transfer of soluble discharge products into shaded collecting water is required.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge energy enables multielectron carbon reduction and C-N bond formation. A balanced selected channel is 2 CO2 + NH3 + 3 H2 -> CH2O + HCN + 3 H2O. This is net precursor accounting, not a claim of selective CO2 hydrogenation without electrical activation.
reactions.reasoning: Schlesinger and Miller (1983) found that sufficiently hydrogen-rich CO2 systems can generate amino-acid precursors, whereas productivity falls sharply as reducing power decreases. This supports a conditional CO2 entry without assuming that a neutral CO2/N2 atmosphere performs comparably to methane-rich experiments. Hydrogen supply, ammonia persistence, and realistic discharge flux remain limiting.

reactions.name: Reversible formaldehyde-ammonia condensation

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich pore water or pool margins at approximately pH 8-9.5. A 0.01-0.1 M formaldehyde-equivalent inventory is a concentrating-pool design window, not a demonstrated environmental abundance. Methanimine is a transient equilibrium species, not an assumed isolable stockpile. Opaque sediment or rock cover limits destructive UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia addition gives a carbinolamine that reversibly dehydrates: CH2O + NH3 <-> CH2NH + H2O. Hydrated formaldehyde, hemiaminal, and oligomeric species compete; cyanide trapping in rxn_005 can draw flux through the low-abundance imine.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports the aldehyde-ammonia-cyanide interpretation of discharge-derived amino acids. The standard imine-first Strecker mechanism does not require a mineral catalyst. Aqueous imine abundance is equilibrium-limited, so this node represents a reactive intermediate rather than evidence for quantitative methanimine accumulation.

reactions.name: Cyanide capture of methanimine

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8-9.5 with available HCN/CN-, ammonia, and carbonyl material. Millimolar-to-tens-of-millimolar cyanide availability is a local concentration assumption. Covered, replenished pores reduce HCN escape; no transition-metal catalyst is added.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine/iminium carbon and proton transfer produces aminoacetonitrile. Net: CH2NH + HCN -> NH2CH2CN.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) provides mechanistic support for Strecker aminonitrile formation; Lerner et al. (1993) independently demonstrated related aqueous Strecker chemistry. The main limitations are reactant supply, cyanide retention, and competing cyanohydrin or polymer formation, not a missing mineral catalyst.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde trapping as glycolonitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 7.5-9.5 in anoxic collecting water. Formaldehyde and cyanide are locally concentrated to millimolar or greater inventories. Retention in shaded pores is preferred over prolonged exposure in an open UV-irradiated film.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the formaldehyde carbonyl followed by proton transfer: CH2O + HCN <-> HOCH2CN.
reactions.reasoning: The aldehyde-cyanide network described by Miller (1957), and the glycolonitrile-centered chemistry discussed by Patel et al. (2015), support this chemically ordinary cyanohydrin branch. Copper, sulfide, and irradiation are not required for cyanohydrin formation from already supplied formaldehyde and cyanide; they are therefore not added as decorative agents.

reactions.name: Ammoniation of the glycolonitrile-equilibrating pool

conditions.other: Ammonia in excess, approximately pH 8-10, with sufficiently long aqueous residence for carbonyl/cyanohydrin/imine equilibration. No rapid direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Net: HOCH2CN + NH3 -> NH2CH2CN + H2O. This is a network-level ammoniation through reversible cyanohydrin dissociation, carbonyl-ammonia chemistry, and cyanide recapture; it is not assigned an unsupported elementary SN2 mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports interconversion within aqueous Strecker precursor pools, and the supplied literature identifies glycolonitrile ammoniation as an equivalent entry to aminoacetonitrile. The route is distinct in precursor capture order but shares the same ultimate aminonitrile. Its flux depends on equilibrium partitioning and ammonia availability rather than on an assumed facile hydroxyl substitution.

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydration to glycinamide
agents: Hydronium supplied by acidic volcanic fluid; homogeneous acid catalysis

conditions.pressure: 10-30 bar, sufficient to retain liquid water
conditions.other: Proposed acidic window pH 1-2, with hours-to-days residence treated as a testable design range rather than a measured rate law. Surface-produced aminonitrile solution infiltrates confined fractures in a volcanic aquifer and mixes with chloride-rich acidic fluid. Transport concerns the less volatile aminonitrile, not preservation of concentrated HCN in an open hot pool.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted nitrile hydration through imidic intermediates: NH2CH2CN + H2O -> NH2CH2CONH2. The amide is represented explicitly even if it does not accumulate substantially under every hydrothermal condition.
reactions.reasoning: Kamaluddin et al. (1979) detected aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide before amino acids in formaldehyde/hydroxylamine chemistry. Hennet et al. (1992) demonstrated net Strecker glycine formation at approximately 423 K and 10 bar. These observations support the intermediate sequence and a hydrothermal processing window, but not a separately measured rate for this exact acidic flow scenario. Natural acid supply and residence time remain bottlenecks; 6 M HCl work-up is not assumed.

reactions.name: Glycinamide hydrolysis and free-glycine release
agents: Hydronium supplied by acidic volcanic fluid; homogeneous acid catalysis

conditions.temperature: 393-423 K during hydrolysis; proposed outlet cooling to below 315 K
conditions.other: Same acidic liquid-water compartment as rxn_008. Residence must be long enough for amide cleavage but short enough to limit glycine degradation and cyclization. A proposed preservation measure is mixing with cooler recharge water within minutes after hot-zone exit; this cooling specification is a scenario requirement, not a reported kinetic result.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed water addition and C-N acyl-bond cleavage: NH2CH2CONH2 + H2O -> NH2CH2COOH + NH3. Under acidic conditions the liberated nitrogen is predominantly ammonium; the equation uses neutral reference species.
reactions.reasoning: Kamaluddin et al. (1979) support glycinamide as an intermediate, while Hennet et al. (1992) support free glycine formation from the overall hydrothermal Strecker system. Resolving amide hydrolysis does not establish its natural environmental rate independently. This is the principal downstream bottleneck in the nitrile pathways, and prolonged hot residence cannot be assumed to preserve the target.

reactions.name: Conditional hydroxylamine-associated tandem aminonitrile formation

conditions.pressure: Approximately 3 bar in a confined aqueous compartment
conditions.other: Approximately pH 5.5. Hydroxylamine and formaldehyde must be concentrated relative to dilute ocean water; ammonia is explicitly supplied as an additional boundary reagent. The supplied report does not establish a productive concentration threshold or a yield for this exact ternary formulation. No Fe(III)-rich modified-seawater recipe is imposed.

reactions.mechanism: Mixture-level oxime formation, cyanide-generating chemistry, and ammonia-assisted aminonitrile capture are represented together. A balanced selected channel is 2 CH2O + NH2OH + NH3 -> NH2CH2CN + 3 H2O. No isolated, high-flux aqueous formaldoxime-dehydration reaction is asserted.
reactions.reasoning: Oró et al. (1959) demonstrated glycine formation from formaldehyde/hydroxylamine mixtures, and Kamaluddin et al. (1979) detected cyanide, aminoacetonitrile, and glycinamide before amino acids. Hatanaka and Egami (1977) provide an approximately 378 K, pH 5.5 experimental anchor, although their metal-containing recipe is not reproduced here. The exact ternary channel and mineral-free conditions encoded here are a mechanistically justified but speculative extrapolation, not an independently validated recipe. Explicit ammonia avoids claiming that this balanced reaction also generates ammonia. Hydroxylamine supply remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Buffered glyoxylate aza-Cannizzaro disproportionation
agents: Phosphate buffer as a proton-transfer medium; no metal or external reductant

conditions.other: Experimental anchor: 0.5 M glyoxylic acid with the reported 0.5 M ammonium-phosphate formulation, approximately pH 7-10, for 48 h. Evaporative concentration must precede reaction while liquid water remains. The pool or pore is shaded after concentration to limit photodestruction. No comparable flux is assumed below approximately 0.25 M glyoxylate.

reactions.mechanism: Glyoxylate-derived imine/hemiaminal partners exchange hydride, reducing one C2 unit to glycine while oxidizing the other to oxamate. Neutral-reference net: 2 C2H2O3 + 2 NH3 -> C2H5NO2 + C2H3NO3 + H2O.
reactions.reasoning: Jarois et al. (2024) reported approximately 11-14% glycine under concentrated, buffered conditions near 323 K, with isotope evidence supporting internal hydride transfer. The buffer is included because unbuffered glyoxylate/NH4OH did not reproduce the result. This is a cyanide-free and external-reductant-free route, but its strong concentration dependence prevents extrapolation to dilute seawater. Glyoxylate production and concentration remain explicit upstream gaps.

reactions.name: Reductive amination by a pre-reduced FeS-Fe0 assemblage
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS-Fe0 assemblage; FeS provides the reactive mineral interface and Fe0 supplies consumed reducing equivalents

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in the experimental analogue
conditions.other: Approximately pH 9.6 for 48 h, with millimolar glyoxylate and excess ammonium. The active laboratory material was pre-reduced at potentials approximately at or below -0.7 V versus SHE. This node represents a cool, shielded mineral interface, not a 350-600 K vent interior. At least one molar equivalent of accessible Fe0 per glycine is required under the displayed Fe(II)-product accounting.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms a glyoxylate-derived imine, which receives two electrons from low-valence iron. A balanced hydroxylated-Fe(II) accounting equation is C2H2O3 + NH3 + Fe + H2O -> C2H5NO2 + Fe(OH)2. The actual Fe(II) product may remain surface-associated or enter other mineral phases.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported up to 59% glycine with electrochemically prepared FeS-Fe0 material under mild alkaline conditions. Fe0 is therefore represented as a consumed reactant rather than an inexhaustible catalyst. Natural formation, reactive surface area, and persistence of an equivalently reduced assemblage are not demonstrated by that yield. The Fe(OH)2 output is redox-component bookkeeping, not a claim that pure ferrous hydroxide was the identified alteration product or that it automatically constitutes active brucite.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination on nickel-bearing metal
agents: Accessible Ni-bearing meteoritic metal, using the Aletai material as an experimental analogue

conditions.other: Approximately 30 mM ketoacid, pH 8 water, ammonium bicarbonate, and 72 h as a representative experimental regime. A closed gas-water pore or mineral-interface reactor retains hydrogen. Cyanide-rich and sulfide-rich streams are excluded from this compartment because metal binding and surface poisoning could suppress activity.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible glyoxylate-ammonia condensation is followed by nickel-mediated H2 activation and imine hydrogenation. Net: C2H2O3 + NH3 + H2 -> C2H5NO2 + H2O. Competing carbonyl reduction can produce hydroxy-acid material and is not counted as glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated H2-driven ketoacid reductive amination with nickel catalysts and Ni-bearing meteorite material, including glycine in glyoxylate-containing networks. Their reported combined amino-acid plus hydroxy-acid yields are not relabeled as glycine-specific yields here. Native or meteoritic nickel is chosen instead of geochemically implausible abundant Pd/C. Hydrogen availability is credible in serpentinizing systems, but exposed catalyst area, passivation, and sustained substrate supply remain open.

reactions.name: Ferroan-brucite reductive amination with supplied ammonia
agents: Ferroan brucite, approximately Fe0.33Mg0.67(OH)2; its accessible Fe(II) inventory is consumed and represented by mol_018

conditions.other: Alkaline mineral-water interface, approximately pH 9-11 as a scenario window, with approximately 100 mM-scale glyoxylate and fixed nitrogen in the experimental family. Incubation extends to six weeks. At least two reactive Fe(II) equivalents are required per glycine after ammonia is available. Brucite composition, site accessibility, and anoxic preservation are prerequisites, not inferred from the mere presence of dissolved Fe2+.

reactions.mechanism: A glyoxylate-ammonia imine is reduced by oxidation of mineral-hosted Fe(II). Component-equivalent net: C2H2O3 + NH3 + 2 Fe(OH)2 -> C2H5NO2 + 2 FeOOH + H2O. Mg-bearing host components are spectators in this redox accounting; no particular bulk oxidation-product phase is asserted.
reactions.reasoning: Chimiak et al. (2024) reported approximately 52-69% recovered glycine in ammonia-supplied ferroan-brucite systems, with approximately 17-27% of glycine mineral-associated. The reaction represents formation of intact glycine, but only its solution-accessible fraction is an immediately available free product; mineral digestion is not added as an environmental release step. Fe(II) is a stoichiometric reductant. Natural formation and persistence of a sufficiently reactive ferroan-brucite inventory remain necessary boundary assumptions.

reactions.name: Ferroan-brucite reduction of nitrate to an ammonia pool
agents: Ferroan brucite, approximately Fe0.33Mg0.67(OH)2; mineral-hosted Fe(II) provides the eight-electron nitrogen reduction

conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline mineral slurry, approximately pH 9-11 as a scenario window, approximately 100 mM initial nitrate and 100 mM glyoxylate in the coupled experiment, incubated for six weeks. This and rxn_014 occur in the same compartment; ammonia need not be isolated or transported. The minimum combined redox budget is ten accessible Fe(II) equivalents per nitrate-derived glycine, before competing reactions.

reactions.mechanism: Multistep nitrate reduction passes through nitrogen-oxide intermediates to reduced nitrogen. Alkaline component-equivalent net: NO3- + 8 Fe(OH)2 -> NH3 + 8 FeOOH + 2 H2O + OH-. Subsequent ammonia capture and two-electron carbon reduction are represented separately by rxn_014.
reactions.reasoning: Chimiak et al. (2024) demonstrated the integrated nitrate/glyoxylate/ferroan-brucite system, with approximately 0.1-3.1% total recovered glycine after six weeks. The isolated nitrate-reduction rate is not inferred from that overall yield. Approximately 71-97% of recovered glycine was mineral-associated, so the soluble target fraction is substantially smaller than the total analytical recovery. Concentrating nitrate to approximately 0.1 M, maintaining enough reactive Fe(II), and distinguishing dissolved from mineral-bound product are major limitations. Nitrate does not imply a molecular-oxygen atmosphere, but its source and concentration are not solved here.

pathways.name: Methane discharge followed by imine-first Strecker synthesis
pathways.description: Methane-rich discharge supplies formaldehyde and HCN. Ammonia condensation and cyanide capture produce aminoacetonitrile, which is transported as an aqueous solute into a confined hot-water hydrolysis compartment. Subsequent cooling preserves free glycine. This resolves upstream precursor production rather than treating the discharge as a direct selective glycine reaction.

pathways.name: Methane discharge followed by cyanohydrin-first Strecker synthesis
pathways.description: Discharge-derived formaldehyde first traps cyanide as glycolonitrile. Equilibration with excess ammonia accesses aminoacetonitrile without assuming direct displacement of hydroxide. This chemically supported branching alternative converges with P1 before hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-rich CO atmosphere to glycine
pathways.description: Electrical activation of CO in a hydrogen-rich, ammonia-containing gas-water system supplies the Strecker precursor pool. This differs from P1 in its upstream carbon feed and reducing-equivalent requirement, while deliberately sharing the experimentally established downstream imine and nitrile chemistry.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-rich CO2 atmosphere to glycine
pathways.description: A transient strongly reducing CO2/H2 gas-water system supplies formaldehyde and cyanide under electrical activation, followed by Strecker synthesis and hydrolysis. The pathway is conditional on substantial hydrogen and does not claim comparable productivity in an ordinary neutral CO2/N2 atmosphere.

pathways.name: Conditional hydroxylamine entry into the aminonitrile pathway
pathways.description: Supplied formaldehyde, hydroxylamine, and ammonia enter a thermally driven aminonitrile-generating mixture, followed by explicit nitrile and amide hydrolysis. Formaldehyde is an allowed boundary substrate as well as a product of rxn_001-rxn_003. Literature supports aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide in related mixtures, but not the exact ternary formulation or a productive isolated oxime-dehydration step. This pathway is not assigned the same evidential status as the established Strecker core.

pathways.name: Concentrated buffered aza-Cannizzaro synthesis
pathways.description: A concentrated glyoxylate/ammonium pool forms glycine by internal hydride transfer, with oxamate as the oxidation coproduct. No cyanide, metal reductant, or hydrogen supply is required. The experimentally important buffer and approximately 0.5 M concentration are retained; the route is not extrapolated to dilute seawater.

pathways.name: Low-valence iron mineral-interface reductive amination
pathways.description: Glyoxylate and supplied ammonia are converted to glycine at a cool FeS-Fe0 interface. Zero-valent iron is explicitly consumed. The demonstrated chemistry is separated from the unresolved geological production of sufficiently reduced and reactive FeS-Fe0 material.

pathways.name: Nickel-catalyzed hydrogen-driven reductive amination
pathways.description: Hydrogen supplies reducing equivalents to a glyoxylate/ammonia mixture on accessible nickel-bearing metal. This cyanide-free pathway occupies its own gas-retaining, low-temperature compartment, avoiding assumed compatibility with cyanide- or sulfide-rich streams.

pathways.name: Ammonia-fed ferroan-brucite glycine synthesis
pathways.description: Supplied ammonia reacts with glyoxylate, and mineral-hosted Fe(II) supplies the two reducing equivalents needed for glycine. A substantial solution-accessible glycine fraction is distinguished from mineral-associated product. Neither mineral oxidation nor product recovery is represented as cost-free catalysis.

pathways.name: Integrated nitrate-to-glycine ferroan-brucite pathway
pathways.description: Within one alkaline mineral compartment, ferroan brucite first reduces nitrate toward ammonia and then supports glyoxylate reductive amination. The sequence is a mechanistic decomposition of a coupled experimental system, not an asserted isolation of ammonia. Ten Fe(II) equivalents per nitrate-derived glycine are required in the displayed accounting. Low total yield, six-week processing, and predominant mineral association limit immediately available free glycine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The discharge-to-Strecker sequence is well supported by Miller's mechanistic work and subsequent experiments. All reactions conserve atoms and charge under the supplied check. Separating surface aminonitrile formation from hotter hydrolysis is chemically sensible. However, the submitted entries do not specify precursor capture, concentrations, transport, or hydrolysis operating windows. Hennet et al. (1992) support hydrothermal Strecker chemistry, but not unrestricted residence at elevated temperature without glycine loss.
suggestions: Specify discharge gas composition, aqueous capture, and the concentration and survival of formaldehyde, cyanide, and ammonia.
Document aminonitrile transport and hydrolysis temperature, pH, liquid-water pressure, residence time, and cooling; verify free glycine before analytical strong-acid treatment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Glycolonitrile formation provides a credible alternative entry into the established Strecker network. The wording of rxn_007 appropriately describes an equilibrating pool: it should not be interpreted as facile direct displacement of hydroxide by ammonia. This branch is chemically coherent, but its conversion and selectivity depend on solution composition. As in P1, the principal implementation gaps concern concentration, transfer, and hydrolysis rather than conservation or target identity.
suggestions: Provide pH, ammonia concentration, and residence time supporting net glycolonitrile-to-aminoacetonitrile conversion through the equilibrating carbonyl/imine pool.
Specify transfer into a validated hydrolysis window and measure glycinamide, free glycine, and competing degradation products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Evaluated using the imine-first downstream branch. Schlesinger and Miller (1983) support electrical-discharge generation of Strecker precursors from sufficiently hydrogen-rich CO mixtures. This is not an unsupported ambient-temperature CO condensation proposal. The balanced net equation does not establish the required experimental gas ratios or precursor yields. Gas composition, discharge exposure, capture, and downstream hydrolysis conditions remain insufficiently specified.
suggestions: State the selected downstream reaction sequence explicitly and attach the relevant CO-discharge citations to rxn_002.
Specify hydrogen and CO partial pressures, energy input, captured precursor concentrations, and transport into the hydrolysis environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Evaluated using the imine-first downstream branch. Hydrogen-rich CO2 discharge chemistry has experimental support in Schlesinger and Miller (1983); CO2 is not intrinsically a disqualifying feedstock. Nevertheless, the inferred stoichiometric hydrogen coefficient is not an atmospheric operating ratio. The submission needs quantitative reducing conditions and aqueous capture information, including the effect of dissolved CO2 on downstream pH. Final hydrolysis remains plausible but operationally under-specified.
suggestions: Specify experimentally supported hydrogen-to-CO2 ratios, partial pressures, discharge exposure, and precursor recovery.
Document aqueous pH control, aminonitrile formation, transport, and hydrolysis without assuming that gas-phase stoichiometry establishes reactor conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The balanced ternary equation is chemically conceivable through oxime formation, cyanide generation, and Strecker capture, but balance does not demonstrate that this exact formulation works. Oro et al. (1959) and Kamaluddin et al. (1979) support related formaldehyde/hydroxylamine chemistry and observed nitrile/amide intermediates, not necessarily the proposed ammonia-supplemented recipe. The conditional designation is appropriate. Its three-step count begins at the formaldehyde hub rather than at a listed boundary feedstock.
suggestions: Test the exact ternary mixture, resolving oxime, cyanide, aminoacetonitrile, glycinamide, and free-glycine formation over time.
Specify temperature, pH, reactant ratios, and any metal additives rather than transferring results indiscriminately from binary-mixture studies.
Include an upstream formaldehyde-supply reaction when describing this as a complete boundary-feedstock-to-target pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest specified branch because Jarois et al. (2024) directly support free-glycine formation by buffered glyoxylate aza-Cannizzaro chemistry, with oxamic acid as the complementary oxidation product. The balanced equation correctly represents internal redox transfer without an external reductant. The concentrated, buffered qualification addresses the central experimental constraint, although the actual concentration, buffer identity, and operating conditions are not included in the reaction entry. Supplied glyoxylate is accepted as a declared boundary resource.
suggestions: Attach an explicit recipe and citation, such as the reported approximately 0.5 M glyoxylate/ammonium-buffer system at 50 degrees C for 48 hours.
Specify buffer identity, pH, and maintenance of concentration; do not extrapolate the reported conversion to dilute or unbuffered solutions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019) directly support glyoxylate reductive amination by an electrochemically pre-reduced FeS-Fe0 assemblage. The network correctly treats low-valence iron as a consumed reductant rather than a perpetually active catalyst. Fe(OH)2 is acceptable as the declared accounting equivalent, not an experimentally identified corrosion phase. The remaining uncertainty concerns the active material's preparation, loading, preservation, and aqueous operating conditions; the label 'Biochemical' does not establish those conditions.
suggestions: Document the active assemblage preparation, including the sufficiently reducing pretreatment and accessible Fe0 inventory.
Specify anoxic handling and a literature-matched operating window, approximately pH 9.6 and 23-25 degrees C for 48 hours in the cited experiment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over active nickel-bearing metal is supported by Kaur et al. (2024). The net equation correctly uses H2 as the reductant and does not require nickel consumption. However, generic nickel content does not establish catalytic activity, and the submission does not provide hydrogen pressure, catalyst preparation, or solution composition. Competition with hydroxy-acid formation affects selectivity but does not invalidate experimentally observed glycine production.
suggestions: Identify the actual active nickel-bearing material, its loading and surface preparation, and controls demonstrating catalytic activity.
Specify pressure, pH, ammonium source, and residence time against the reported approximately 5 bar H2, pH 8, 22 degrees C, 72-hour experimental anchor.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chimiak et al. (2024) provide direct experimental support for ammonia-fed ferroan-brucite glycine synthesis. Two Fe(II) equivalents per reductive amination correctly supply the required electrons. The component-equivalent treatment is acceptable and does not imply that rxn_012 corrosion products are active brucite. The main gaps are mineral composition/loading, reactant concentrations, reaction duration, and product partitioning. Mineral-associated glycine still satisfies the molecular target, but should be distinguished from dissolved product.
suggestions: Specify ferroan-brucite composition, accessible Fe(II) loading, pH, temperature, and incubation time.
Maintain an environment-specific fresh-brucite inventory and report dissolved versus mineral-associated glycine separately.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The integrated nitrate-to-glycine system is directly supported by Chimiak et al. (2024), rather than merely inferred by joining unrelated experiments. The eight-Fe(II) nitrate-reduction coefficient is chemically appropriate; combining both reactions requires ten Fe(II) equivalents per glycine at ideal stoichiometry. Important implementation constraints are the approximately 100 mM reactants, six-week incubation, modest conversion, and substantial mineral association. These observations establish glycine formation but not a large freely dissolved glycine inventory.
suggestions: Provide a coupled nitrogen and electron budget, including accessible mineral Fe(II), nitrate conversion, ammonia availability, and competing reduction products.
Specify concentration maintenance and six-week mineral/reactant retention under the intended aqueous conditions.
Distinguish directly dissolved glycine from mineral-associated glycine recovered during work-up; do not count the latter automatically as freely available product.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has sufficient nodes, consistent molecular identities, and a connected reaction graph. The deterministic conservation check is accepted: eight reactions are balanced as listed and seven are balanceable with reasonable coefficients; none violates atom or charge conservation. Atmospheric reactions are acceptable lumped precursor-supply equations, not elementary mechanisms or quantitative yield predictions. Literature alignment is strong for the Strecker, aza-Cannizzaro, FeS-Fe0, H2/Ni, and ferroan-brucite systems. Several supported branches genuinely produce glycine, and the explicitly conditional hydroxylamine branch does not negate those routes. Declared feedstock and mineral inventories are accepted as boundary resources, without assuming upstream closure or mineral regeneration. Nevertheless, the supplied reaction entries lack the numerical operating conditions, reaction-level citations, and physical transfer specifications needed to verify the complete implementation. Hydrolysis kinetics and preservation, active mineral preparation, and dissolved-versus-mineral-associated product accounting remain important gaps. P3 and P4 were evaluated through the imine-first branch because their reaction sequences were not explicitly enumerated. Flagged reactions require additional substantiation or condition specification; none is flagged for conservation failure. Route count, shared hubs, and environmental ordering were not scoring advantages or disadvantages. The network is credible but does not meet the 0.90 network-approval threshold as submitted.
